newsitem.title: USA: Court approves settlement of Prudential life insurance suit.
newsitem.headline: Court approves settlement of Prudential life insurance suit.

text.p: A federal judge Monday approved an offer by Prudential Insurance Co. of America to pay at least $410 million to policy holders to settle a class-action dispute over the insurer's sales practices.
In the decision, U.S. District Judge Alfred Wolin directed Prudential to begin notifying class members that the settlement has been approved by no later than March 15.
Under the settlement, people who purchased as many as 10.7 million permanent life insurance policies between 1982 and 1995 will be eligible for restitution.
The settlement could cost Prudential as much as $1.2 billion and have a total value to policyholders of nearly $2 billion.
"We're gratified at the judge's decision and it enables us to move forward quickly in resolving our policyowners' problems," a Prudential spokesman said.
Although company officials see the settlement approval as an important milestone, they said they still have a way to go before its sales practice problems are completely behind it.
The company still must resolve the cases of several hundred policyholders who chose not to participate in the class action settlement.

"We're disappointed, but not surprised," said Michael Malakoff, a Pittsburgh policyholder attorney who opposed the settlement. He said he expects to appeal the decision after the court renders its full opinion.
In addition, the company may face various other state suits.
Policyholders who chose to participate in the class-action settlement and who have clear-cut cases may receive remedies within the next several months, Prudential said.

Policyholders began receiving notices in February about the opportunity to receive remediation if they were misled by the company's sales agents. They have until June 1 to decide between one of two types of relief.

One offers policyholders, at no cost, the potential for at least a partial refund of their premiums, plus interest. The other offers policyholders enhanced life insurance, annuities and low-cost premium loans.

In their complaints, policyholders claimed that Prudential sales agents misled them into replacing old policies with newer, more expensive ones or into buying new policies that did not perform as promised.
Prudential is not the only U.S. insurer to face complaints about its life insurance sales practices in recent years.

Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., New York Life Insurance Co. and Allianz Life Insurance Co. of North America, a unit of Germany's Allianz AG Holding, all have been involved in similar actions in the last two years.

Metropolitan Life agreed in 1994 to pay $20 million in fines and up to $76 million in policyholder refunds to settle allegations it improperly marketed life insurance policies as retirement or savings plans.
New York Life last year agreed to a national class action settlement in a dispute over dividends on life insurance policies.
Allianz Life agreed in June to pay $5.1 million, including $2.3 million in restitution, to settle allegations it engaged in deceptive sales practices in California.
